conditions.title: Heart Failure
conditions.definition: The heart can no longer pump enough blood to meet the body's needs.
patho: The heart muscle weakens or stiffens
Cardiac output drops
The body compensates: RAAS activates, sodium and water are retained, the heart enlarges and beats faster
Over time the compensation fails
Blood backs up behind the failing side of the heart

signs.s: Left HF: crackles, dyspnea, orthopnea, pink frothy sputum
signs.why: Blood backs up into the lungs (Left = Lungs)

signs.s: Right HF: JVD, peripheral edema, ascites, weight gain
signs.why: Blood backs up into the systemic veins (Right = Rest of body)
Low cardiac output means less oxygen to tissues

conditions.title: Myocardial Infarction (MI)
conditions.definition: Death of heart muscle caused by a sudden loss of coronary blood flow.
patho: A plaque ruptures in a coronary artery
A clot forms and blocks blood flow
The heart muscle beyond the blockage becomes ischemic (starved of oxygen)
If flow isn't restored within minutes to hours, those cells die (infarct)

signs.s: Crushing chest pain radiating to the arm/jaw
signs.why: Ischemic myocardium releases pain signals
Sympathetic 'fight or flight' response
The failing pump backs blood into the lungs

signs.s: Atypical/silent symptoms in women & older adults
signs.why: Blunted or different pain perception

conditions.title: COPD
conditions.definition: Chronic, progressive airflow limitation from chronic bronchitis and/or emphysema.
patho: Chronic airway irritation causes inflammation and excess mucus (bronchitis) and destroys alveolar walls (emphysema)
Airways narrow and alveoli lose their elastic recoil
Air becomes trapped and can't be fully exhaled
Gas exchange fails → CO₂ is retained and oxygen falls

signs.why: Air trapping makes exhaling hard
Excess mucus from chronic bronchitis
Chronic air trapping enlarges the chest
The client instinctively keeps airways open longer

conditions.title: Pneumonia
conditions.definition: Infection and inflammation of the lung tissue, filling alveoli with fluid and pus.
patho: A pathogen reaches the alveoli
The immune system triggers inflammation
Alveoli fill with exudate and pus (consolidation)
Gas exchange across the alveoli is impaired

signs.why: Immune response to infection

signs.s: Crackles and dullness over the affected lobe
signs.why: Fluid-filled, consolidated alveoli
Impaired gas exchange
Hypoxia and infection affect the brain

conditions.title: Diabetes Mellitus
conditions.definition: Chronic high blood glucose from lack of insulin (Type 1) or insulin resistance (Type 2).
causes: Type 1: autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
Type 2: insulin resistance + relative deficiency (obesity, genetics)
patho: Insulin is absent or ineffective
Glucose can't move from the blood into the cells
Blood glucose rises (hyperglycemia) while the cells starve
High blood glucose spills into the urine and drags water with it (osmotic diuresis)

signs.why: Glucose in the urine pulls water out osmotically
The body is dehydrated from fluid loss
Cells are starved of glucose despite high blood levels

signs.s: Fatigue, blurred vision, slow wound healing
signs.why: Cells lack fuel; high glucose damages vessels/nerves

complications: Chronic: neuropathy, nephropathy, retinopathy, heart disease

conditions.title: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA)
conditions.definition: A life-threatening complication of diabetes: severe hyperglycemia with ketosis and acidosis.
patho: Without insulin, cells can't use glucose for energy
The body breaks down fat instead, producing ketones (acids)
Ketones build up → metabolic acidosis
Meanwhile hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis → dehydration and electrolyte loss

signs.why: The lungs blow off CO₂ to compensate for the acidosis
Ketones (acetone) are exhaled
Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia
Acidosis and dehydration affect GI and brain

diagnostics: pH <7.3, low bicarbonate, high anion gap
complications: Hypokalemia (as insulin drives K⁺ into cells)
treatment: Replace potassium; monitor glucose, K⁺, and pH

conditions.title: Chronic Kidney Disease
conditions.definition: Progressive, irreversible loss of kidney function over months to years.
patho: Nephrons are progressively and permanently damaged
The glomerular filtration rate (GFR) falls
The kidneys can no longer clear wastes, balance fluid/electrolytes, make erythropoietin, or activate vitamin D
Wastes accumulate (uremia); fluid and electrolytes build up

signs.why: The kidneys can't excrete sodium and water
Low erythropoietin → anemia
Uremia — waste products accumulate in the blood
Failing kidneys can't excrete potassium

treatment: Renal diet: limit protein, potassium, phosphorus, sodium, fluid
Phosphate binders, erythropoietin, dialysis or transplant

conditions.title: Sepsis
conditions.definition: Life-threatening organ dysfunction from the body's dysregulated response to infection.
causes: Any infection (pneumonia, UTI, wound, IV line)
patho: An infection triggers a massive, body-wide inflammatory response
Widespread vasodilation and leaky capillaries develop
Blood pressure and tissue perfusion drop
Cells become hypoxic → organ dysfunction; unchecked, it becomes septic shock

signs.why: Systemic inflammatory response

signs.s: Warm, flushed skin early → cool and mottled late
signs.why: Vasodilation first, then failing perfusion

signs.s: New confusion and decreased urine output
signs.why: Poor perfusion to the brain and kidneys
Tissues switch to anaerobic metabolism; distributive shock

treatment: Cultures THEN broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour
Vasopressors if needed; source control; monitor lactate

conditions.title: Stroke (CVA)
conditions.definition: Interruption of blood flow to part of the brain, causing neuron death.
causes: Ischemic (≈87%): clot or atherosclerosis; emboli from atrial fibrillation
Hemorrhagic: hypertension or a ruptured aneurysm
patho: Blood flow to an area of brain is blocked (ischemic) or a vessel ruptures (hemorrhagic)
Neurons in that area are deprived of oxygen and glucose
Brain cells begin to die within minutes
The functions that region controlled are lost

signs.s: Sudden facial droop, arm weakness, slurred speech (FAST)
signs.why: The affected brain region can't control those functions
Motor and language centers are damaged
Bleeding raises intracranial pressure
Cranial nerve/brainstem involvement → aspiration risk

diagnostics: CT scan FIRST (rules out bleed before any clot-buster)
treatment: Ischemic: tPA within the window (only if CT shows no bleed), then antiplatelets

conditions.title: Cirrhosis
conditions.definition: Irreversible scarring (fibrosis) of the liver that replaces healthy tissue.
patho: Chronic liver injury causes ongoing inflammation
Healthy liver tissue is replaced by scar tissue (fibrosis)
Scarring blocks blood flow through the liver → portal hypertension
The liver can no longer detoxify, make proteins/clotting factors, or process bilirubin

signs.why: The liver can't process bilirubin
Low albumin + portal hypertension push fluid into the abdomen
The liver can't make clotting factors
Ammonia builds up → hepatic encephalopathy
Portal hypertension backs up into esophageal veins

treatment: Low sodium + diuretics and paracentesis for ascites
Lactulose for ammonia; beta-blockers for varices; bleeding precautions
